summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys the Muslim world and its cultural and intellectual contributions. It covers the size and linguistic diversity of the Muslim population, Islamic philosophy and medicine (Ibn Sina, Ibn al-Nafis, al-Zahrawi), and influence on Western literature (Ibn Tufail, One Thousand and One Nights, Dante, Shakespeare). It also notes achievements in architecture, trade and agriculture, and defines the term Muslim world and the Ummah.
one_line: Overview of the Muslim world's population, its scholarly, literary, architectural and trade contributions, and the meaning of the term Ummah.
key_facts: More than 20% of the world's population is Muslim, with an estimated 1.5 billion Muslims.
Muslims are the majority in 49 countries and speak hundreds of languages.
Ibn Sina (Avicenna) (980–1037) had more than 450 books attributed to him, mostly on philosophy and medicine.
Avicenna's The Canon of Medicine was used as the standard text in European universities for centuries and remained authoritative in Europe until the 18th century.
Ibn al-Nafis, an Egyptian physician, proposed the theory of pulmonary circulation.
Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (Abulcasis) contributed to medical surgery with his Kitab al-Tasrif ('Book of Concessions').
Ibn Tufail's philosophical novel Hayy ibn Yaqdha was translated into Latin as Philosophus Autodidactus in 1671.
Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, regarded as the first novel in English, may have been inspired by translations of Ibn Tufail's work.
One Thousand and One Nights was first translated into Western languages in the 18th century, first by Antoine Galland.
Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy drew on Arabic works on Islamic eschatology, including the Kitab al-Miraj.
Theologus Autodidactus by Ibn al-Nafis (1213–1288) is described as the first example of a science fiction novel.
The Dome of the Rock mosque, first appearing in 691, is the earliest example of the domes used across centuries of Islamic architecture.
Arab merchants dominated Indian Ocean trade until the arrival of the Portuguese in the 16th century.
In a religious sense, the Islamic Ummah refers to those who adhere to the teachings of Islam, referred to as Muslims.
The term Ummah means 'nation' or 'community' in Arabic.
